title: Three psychologists measured who actually notices you
_format: 1080x1350 = 4:5. NICHT 3:4 — die Instagram-API akzeptiert beim automatischen Veroeffentlichen nur 4:5 bis 1.91:1. Bildprompts bleiben 3:4, ihre schwarze Fusszone faengt die Differenz ab.
_syntax: [Klammern] = Akzentfarbe mit Textur (nur in headline). **Sterne** = fett in bullets/body. Zeilenumbruch = eigener Array-Eintrag. `alt` pro Slide ist Pflicht — Buffer verlangt altText beim Upload.

caption.kern: Three psychologists put a student in a Barry Manilow t-shirt, walked him into a room full of strangers, then counted who actually noticed. He guessed exactly twice the real number. 👕😬
caption.detail: Thomas Gilovich, Victoria Husted Medvec and Kenneth Savitsky ran it at Cornell as Study 1 of the paper that named the spotlight effect. The wearers estimated 46% of the room could say who was on the shirt. Then the observers were asked. 23% could. Per session, each wearer overshot their own room by 23 percentage points.
caption.kontext: The mechanism is anchoring and adjustment: you start from how loud the shirt is in your own head, then adjust down for other people — never far enough. They proved it by making students sit in the shirt for 15 minutes before entering. Same shirt, same room. Sent in immediately, they guessed 51%. After getting used to it, 37%. And when students wore a shirt they were proud of — Marley, Seinfeld, Martin Luther King Jr. — they guessed 48% while only 8% could name the face. Being pleased with it made the gap six times wider, not smaller.
caption.frage: What is the moment you still cringe about that nobody else remembers?
caption.sources: Sources: Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky — The spotlight effect in social judgment: an egocentric bias in estimates of the salience of one's own actions and appearance • Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 78(2): 211–222, February 2000 • doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.78.2.211

slides.alt: A folded t-shirt lying alone under a single hard overhead light on a dark table, the print on it turned away from the camera. Headline: Three psychologists sent a student into a room in an embarrassing shirt to count who actually noticed.

headline: AT [CORNELL], THEY HANDED HIM
A SHIRT WITH [BARRY MANILOW] ON IT
slides.body: Then they walked him into a room where [five strangers] sat filling out forms — and pulled him back out seconds later.
slides.alt: A young man standing in a doorway of a bright university seminar room, seen from behind, several students at a table ahead of him with their heads down over paperwork. Headline: At Cornell, they handed him a shirt with Barry Manilow on it.

headline: HE GUESSED [46%].
THE ROOM SAID [23%].
slides.body: You start from how loud it is [inside your own head], then adjust down for other people — [never far enough]. Psychologists call it [anchoring and adjustment].
slides.alt: A hallway outside a closed door, one figure waiting alone against the wall under a warm wall lamp, the corridor falling away into darkness. Headline: He guessed 46 percent. The room said 23 percent.

headline: SO THEY MADE [STUDENTS]
WAIT [15 MINUTES] IN THE SHIRT
slides.body: Same shirt, same room, same strangers. Sent in immediately they guessed [51%]. After getting used to it, [37%]. Nothing changed but [how loudly they felt it].
slides.alt: A person sitting alone at a long empty computer lab desk under fluorescent light, a clock on the wall behind them, an unfinished survey in front of them. Headline: So they made students wait 15 minutes in the shirt.

headline: THEN THEY TRIED [A SHIRT]
THE STUDENTS [LIKED]
slides.body: Marley. Seinfeld. [Martin Luther King]. The wearers guessed [48%] — [8%] could name the face. [Six times] off.
slides.alt: Three folded t-shirts stacked on a wooden bench in warm light, their prints creased and unreadable. Headline: Then they tried a shirt the students liked.
